reception.text: Washington State papers that reported the 1905 auction of the old Fort Sherman grounds said nothing about the cemetery grant, and no press notice of the proclamation has been found.
reception.source: Chewelah Independent, June 9, 1905; Pullman Herald, June 10, 1905 (Washington Digital Newspapers)

political_impact.text: The proclamation answered a petition from the citizens of Coeur d'Alene, granting the town 19.45 acres, which already held the old post's burying ground, for a public cemetery.
political_impact.source: Proclamation 545, 34 Stat. 3004; City of Coeur d'Alene Cemetery Division

legacy.text: The tract is today's Forest Cemetery on North Government Way, run by the city, which later bought neighboring land for Riverview Cemetery.
legacy.source: City of Coeur d'Alene Cemetery Division

legacy.text: Most of the rest of the old post was sold at public auction in 1905, much of it to the Stack and Gibbs Lumber Company; North Idaho College moved to the fort site in 1949.
legacy.source: Idaho State Historical Society, Reference Series No. 355; North Idaho College history page

today.name: Forest Cemetery, Coeur d'Alene
today.note: City-run cemetery at 1011 North Government Way.
today.source: City of Coeur d'Alene Cemetery Division

uncertain: A 2021 Coeur d'Alene Press account describes the grant as one acre of the old post cemetery plus 19.7 added acres, which does not match the proclamation's single 19.45-acre lot; the plat would resolve it.

reception.text: A search of California papers, including the San Diego Union, for May through July 1905 found no notice of the restoration.

political_impact.text: The restoration cleared the way for Joseph J. Henderson, who had lived on part of Section 5 since March 10, 1895, to file a homestead claim on the land.

related.note: The 1902 proclamation used the same mechanism to release neighboring Section 7 of the Capitan Grande lands for the settler Jacob Kuhner.

uncertain: Who asked for the restoration (Henderson, the General Land Office or the Indian Office) is not known.
What became of Sections 5 and 6 and of Henderson's homestead claim after restoration is not known.

legacy.text: The surviving Fort Sherman post chapel, built around 1880, is part of the Fort Sherman Buildings listing on the National Register of Historic Places.
